title: Sebonac Creek Settlement / Seponack
summary: Seponack, also Sabonac, is recorded as a neck of land at Southampton on Peconic Bay. The name also connects the related Sebonac Creek Settlement and the Sabonack cross-reference.
map_geometry_source: Public orientation point from OpenStreetMap/Nominatim for Sebonac Creek; not an exact settlement boundary.
why_this_matters: Archaeological evidence from this Shinnecock settlement, including the remains of a fifteen-by-twenty-foot wigwam and a pottery fragment bearing a Thunderbird design, offers a rare, intimate glimpse into early domestic and spiritual life. Preserving the memory of these deeply rooted village spaces allows modern observers to appreciate the rich, everyday cultural practices of Algonquian communities long before European contact.
history_content: The place appears in Southampton records as Seponack, Seaponack, Sebonack, and related forms. It is associated with Seaponack old ground, Sebonac Neck, Sebonac Creek, and the broader Shinnecock Hills landscape.
translation_content:
Seponack is interpreted as "ground-nut place," from a word for ground-nut and a place suffix. It is connected with Sagaponack and Ketchaponack.

Why Place Names Matter

“Indigenous place names exist as a system. They relate to one another and function as a chain of experiences and stories.”

— Ekaterina Mikhailova, The Importance of Indigenous Place Names (2025), A Living Tradition section
artifacts_content: A splayed bird image was found on pottery fragment excavated at the Sebonac site, which has been identified as a thunder-being symbol. [1. Strong, John A. The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island: From Earliest times to 1700. Interlaken NY: Empire State, 1997. Print.  pp 53] This motif is seen as part of the Shinnecock religion. The Thunderbird is a race of mythic beings who were thought to be the patrons of warriors, the bringers of rain for the crops, and the guardians of mankind against water monsters. Unfortunately, there has been no corroborative data from other Sebonac sites. It seems quite likely, however, that the Thunderbird was known and honored on Long Island because the symbol has been documented among the other coastal Algonkin tribes. [1. Stone, Gaynell. The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History. Stony Brook, NY: Suffolk County Archaeological Association, 1983. Print. pp 23]
excavation_content:
The Sebonac site was excavated by Harrington in 1904, providing an early archaeological picture of cultural changes on Long Island from the Transitional stage into the Woodland period. One of the most important discoveries at Sebonac is the evidence of housing uncovered by Harrington. This was probably the first such find associated with Native cultures on Long Island. The excavation also documented evidence of Native housing on Long Island. Later interpretation describes Harrington's finds:
One of the most spectacular discoveries made by Harrington at the Sebonac site may seem rather mundane at first glance. He found evidence of dwellings. It is spectacular only because so little evidence of structures has been found on Long Island. Harrington located an oval shaped area of stained earth about fifteen feet wide by twenty feet long with a hearth in the center. The stained floor was located about two and a half to three foot below the surface. About ten feet away he excavated a second stained oval are about ten by fifteen feet. No post molds were noted in the report. (Strong 1983:27)
Harrington went on to consult members of the local survive native cultures to help explain the structure size. Wickam Cuffee had remembered as a child seeing structures called "wigwams" and described to Harrington how they were made:
According to Cuffee and other Shinnecock informants, the wigwams were domed shaped structures formed by bending poles toward the center and typing them together. Woven mats as well as thatching were used to cover the frame. A vent was left open over the hearth (strong 1983: 27)
Later on archaeologist such as Werner at Strong's Neck and Gramly and Gwynne at Pipestave Hollow would find similar evidence of structures such as the wigwam in use for the Late Woodland Period. For the first time we have clues to the types of housing being utilized by the Indigenous cultures of Long Island. It appears from this scant evidence that many variations on the wigwam existed, differentiated by such elements such as size and overall shape. Most likely, these fluctuated with the needs of the individuals who built them. [1. Lynch, Thomas. Topology, Climate, and Site Distribution of Three Main Phases of Native Occupation on Long Island, NY, 2001. Print. pp 147]
